metadata.title: Does Claude "Approve" a KYC Packet — or Just Parse It?
metadata.purpose: NikBearBrown (Teardown) cut of claude-liam-kyc-doc-parse: take the kyc-doc-parse skill apart, explain how extraction actually works, and judge the design choice to split parsing from deciding — parse fidelity in the skill, verdict in the downstream rules engine.

beats.narration_text: Watch this. Someone asks whether Claude approves a KYC packet — because kyc-doc-parse sounds like the approval step. It isn't. It's an extractor. The approving happens somewhere else entirely. Liam, in for Bear.

beats.narration_text: The natural guess: kyc-doc-parse looks at a packet and decides — clears the client, or flags them as risky. That is not what it does. It extracts. It reads what is already on the page and drops it into five fixed fields: identity, ownership, control, source of funds, document inventory. Feed it a packet where the beneficial-owner section is blank, and it doesn't sound an alarm — it writes 'missing' in that slot and hands back the rest, parsed exactly as told. They optimized for extraction fidelity over judgment: the skill will never invent what isn't there, and it will never decide what isn't its job.

shot.new_visual_element: A 'clear / flag' decision box, struck; a five-field extraction, lit

production_viz.label: Decides, or extracts?
production_viz.mechanic: Left: a card labelled 'CLEAR OR FLAG?' with a checkmark/X pair beneath it. Right: a card labelled 'FIVE FIELDS, EXTRACTED' listing the five field categories. The left side dims and gets a terracotta strike; the right stays lit. A final line reads 'beneficial owner blank -- recorded as missing, not flagged' and sits outside the card.

beats.narration_text: Here's what's actually happening. Read one onboarding packet, then sort what is in it into five buckets — identity, ownership, control, source of funds, document inventory. Watch the anchor: one packet's data landing across all five slots at once. Nothing here judges the client; the skill only structures what the document says, so a downstream rules engine gets something clean to screen. They split the job on purpose — parsing is deterministic and auditable, and deciding lives in the rules engine, where you can read the rule and change it.

shot.new_visual_element: THE ANCHOR -- one onboarding packet's data landing in all five field buckets

production_viz.label: THE ANCHOR -- one packet, five fields
production_viz.mechanic: THE ANCHOR. Five stacked cards labelled 'IDENTITY', 'OWNERSHIP', 'CONTROL', 'SOURCE OF FUNDS', 'DOCUMENT INVENTORY'. A single highlighted token 'ONBOARDING PACKET' fades in beside each card in turn as its field lights up, never judging, only landing. THIS EXACT COMPOSITION RETURNS, PAID OFF, AT B03.

beats.narration_text: The packet comes out the other side as five filled-in fields — the anchor lands. But a full set of fields isn't a cleared client; it's captured data waiting on the rules engine to actually screen it. And a field marked missing isn't proof of fraud either — the document might just not have been submitted yet. The parse itself never renders the verdict, in either direction. This works if you value repeatability: same packet in, same fields out, every run, and someone else — the rules engine, a reviewer, a policy — decides what those fields mean. It fails the moment you were hoping the skill itself would tell you whether the client is clean.

beats.narration_text: Your turn. Here's a prompt you can paste directly into Claude, ChatGPT, or Gemini — no CLI, nothing installed. Ask it to take a messy document — a lease, an invoice, an onboarding form, whatever is on your desk — read it, and sort the information into five fields you specify in advance. Tell it to quote the source text for each field. And tell it that when a field is genuinely blank, it writes 'MISSING' in that slot instead of guessing what was probably there. Watching a model draw the line between extracting and inventing is the whole lesson. Go deeper: what breaks if you add a sixth field that asks it to judge whether the terms look 'reasonable' — and how does the same-input-same-output guarantee survive, or not, once a slot asks for judgment instead of extraction? Liam, in for Bear.

llm_exercise.prompt: I want to understand the extract-vs-decide split as a skill design pattern. Take the document I paste next — a lease, an invoice, a client onboarding form, whatever I have on hand. Read it and sort the information into these five fields: identity of the parties, ownership or control structure, source of the money involved, key dates and obligations, and a document inventory of everything I attached. For each field, quote the exact source text you used. If a field is genuinely blank in what I sent, write 'MISSING' in that slot rather than guessing what was probably there — the missing entries are as much of the answer as the filled ones. Do not decide anything about the document; only structure what it says.
